citation: Rio E, van Ark M, Docking S, et al. (2017). Isometric Contractions Are More Analgesic Than Isotonic Contractions for Patellar Tendon Pain: An In-Season Randomized Clinical Trial. Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine.
population: 20 jumping athletes (volleyball and basketball), aged >16 years (mean 22.5 ± 4.7 years), 18 men, with clinically diagnosed patellar tendinopathy, participating in games/trainings 3 times per week.
intervention: Isometric leg extension holds at 60° knee flexion (80% maximal voluntary isometric contraction) vs. isotonic leg extension (80% 8-repetition maximum), 4 times per week for 4 weeks; time under load and rest between sets matched.
outcome_measures: Pain (0-10 numerical rating score) during single-leg decline squat (SLDS) measured pre- and post-intervention sessions
VISA-P questionnaire (tendon pain and function) at baseline and after 4 weeks
summary: This in-season randomized trial compared immediate analgesic effects of isometric versus isotonic quadriceps contractions in 20 jumping athletes with patellar tendinopathy. Both protocols reduced pain over 4 weeks, but isometric holds produced significantly greater immediate analgesia during each session.
key_findings: Baseline median SLDS pain was 5/10 in both groups (isotonic range 1–8, isometric range 2–8).
Isometric contractions produced significantly greater immediate analgesia than isotonic contractions (P < 0.05).
Both protocols were efficacious for reducing pain over the 4-week trial.
Greater immediate analgesia from isometric contractions may increase the ability to load or perform.
limitations: Small sample size (n=20) limits generalizability; only in-season jumping athletes studied; abstract only with no full-text details on randomization, blinding, or adherence; immediate analgesia measured but long-term tendon health not assessed.
